title: Python Basics
subtitle: Types, lists, dicts and the everyday tools

cards.prompt: What type is the result of `3 / 2` in Python 3?
cards.note: `/` always performs float division, so `3 / 2` gives 1.5. For integer division use `//`: `3 // 2` is 1.

cards.prompt: What does `7 // 2` evaluate to?
cards.note: `//` is floor division and rounds towards minus infinity, which is why `-7 // 2` gives -4. The remainder comes from `7 % 2`, which is 1.

cards.prompt: Which of these types is immutable: list, dict, set or tuple?
cards.note: A tuple cannot be changed after it is created. That is why it can serve as a dict key, while a list cannot.

cards.prompt: Which list comprehension gives the squares of 0 to 4?
cards.note: The shape is `[expression for item in iterable if condition]`. With round brackets you get a generator instead, which computes values only on demand.

cards.prompt: How do you read `d["x"]` without a `KeyError`, with 0 as the default?
cards.note: Without a second argument, `get` simply returns `None`. If you want to store the default in the dict at the same time, use `d.setdefault("x", 0)`.

cards.prompt: How do you loop over the keys and values of a dict at the same time?
cards.note: `for k, v in d.items():` unpacks each pair directly. Since Python 3.7, dicts are guaranteed to keep insertion order.

cards.prompt: How do you insert the variable `name` into an f-string?
cards.note: Any expression fits in the braces, for example `{price:.2f}` for two decimal places. Since Python 3.8, `{x=}` shows both name and value, handy for debugging.

cards.prompt: What does `with open("a.txt") as f:` guarantee?
cards.note: `with` uses a context manager: cleanup happens when the block exits, even if an exception is raised. The same pattern works for locks and database connections.

cards.prompt: Which keyword turns a function into a generator?
cards.note: A generator hands out values one at a time and remembers its state between calls. That way you can process huge files line by line without loading everything into memory.

cards.prompt: How do you catch a division by zero?
cards.note: Catch exceptions as specifically as possible instead of a bare `except:`. Otherwise you also swallow real bugs and even Ctrl+C.

cards.prompt: Which block always runs, whether or not an exception occurs?
cards.note: `else` runs only if no exception happened; `finally` runs in every case. Ideal for cleanup when you can't use `with`.

cards.prompt: Which keyword do you use to raise an exception yourself?
cards.note: For example `raise ValueError("age must be positive")`. Pick a fitting built-in type or derive your own class from `Exception`.

cards.prompt: How do you create a virtual environment in the `.venv` folder?
cards.note: Activate it with `source .venv/bin/activate` on macOS and Linux or `.venv\Scripts\activate` on Windows. That way every project has its own package versions.

cards.prompt: How do you install the `requests` package?
cards.note: `python -m pip` is the safer form because it is guaranteed to use the pip of the current Python. Install into an active venv rather than globally.

cards.prompt: How do you write the installed packages to a file?
cards.note: On another machine, `pip install -r requirements.txt` restores everything. That way your project runs with the same versions everywhere.

cards.prompt: What does `len([1, [2, 3], 4])` return?
cards.note: `len` only counts the top level. The inner list `[2, 3]` is a single element.

cards.prompt: What does `"abc"[::-1]` give?
cards.note: Slicing has the form `[start:stop:step]`. A step of -1 walks backwards, the quickest way to reverse a string.

cards.prompt: What does `[10, 20, 30][-1]` give?
cards.note: Negative indices count from the end. `-1` is the last element, `-2` the second to last.

cards.prompt: Which value stands for "nothing" in Python?
cards.note: Test with `x is None`, not with `==`. There is exactly one `None` object, so the identity check is correct and faster.

cards.prompt: What does `bool([])` return?
cards.note: Empty containers, 0, `""` and `None` are falsy. That is why idiomatic code says `if not items:` instead of `if len(items) == 0:`.

cards.prompt: Which method adds a single element to the end of a list?
cards.note: `append` adds one element, `extend` adds all elements of another list. So `xs.append([1, 2])` adds a whole list as a single element.

cards.prompt: What is the simplest way to remove duplicates from the list `xs`?
cards.note: A set stores each element only once but loses the order. `list(dict.fromkeys(xs))` keeps it.

cards.prompt: Which built-in function gives you index and value together while iterating?
cards.note: `for i, name in enumerate(names, start=1):` counts from 1. It reads far better than `range(len(names))`.

cards.prompt: Which function walks through two lists in parallel?
cards.note: `zip(names, ages)` yields pairs and stops at the shorter list. `dict(zip(keys, values))` builds a dict in one go.

cards.prompt: How do you write an anonymous function that doubles `x`?
cards.note: Lambdas suit short expressions such as `sorted(people, key=lambda p: p.age)`. Anything longer belongs in a regular `def` function.

cards.prompt: What does `if __name__ == "__main__":` check?
cards.note: On import, `__name__` holds the module name; when run directly it is `"__main__"`. That way test code only runs when you start the file yourself.

cards.prompt: How do you get the number of characters in the string `s`?
cards.note: `len` works on strings, lists, dicts and anything that implements `__len__`. For strings, Python counts Unicode characters, not bytes.

cards.prompt: How do you join `["a", "b", "c"]` into the string `"a,b,c"`?
cards.note: `join` is a method of the separator, not the list, which trips up almost everyone. The reverse is `"a,b,c".split(",")`.

cards.prompt: Which data structure looks up an entry by key in O(1) on average?
cards.note: Dicts are hash tables. `x in some_list` has to scan everything, while `x in some_dict` or `x in some_set` jumps straight to the entry.

cards.prompt: What do you call `@lru_cache` placed above a function definition?
cards.note: A decorator is a function that wraps another function. `@lru_cache` from `functools` remembers results so expensive calls only compute once.
